title: Snapshots of ATP-driven substrate translocation by the mitochondrial AAA+ protease AFG3L2.
abstract: AFG3L2, located in the mitochondrial inner membrane, is an ATP-fueled protease responsible for protein degradation, and its dysfunction has been implicated in multiple neurodegenerative disorders. However, the structural basis underlying its ATP-driven substrate translocation remains incompletely understood. Here, we purified full-length human AFG3L2 and determined its cryo-EM structures in four distinct conformational states (Con1-Con4), revealing substrate engagement in the core catalytic domain despite weak EM density for its transmembrane domain. These structures display an asymmetric spiral-staircase architecture in which the six protomers are arranged around a central pore that accommodates a polypeptide substrate. The four conformational states jointly reveal a substrate translocation mechanism in which ATP binding by the uppermost protomer promotes substrate engagement, whereas ATP hydrolysis by the lowermost ATP-bound protomer leads to substrate release. Our findings provide snapshots of ATP-driven substrate translocation by AFG3L2 and refine the hand-over-hand translocation mechanism by revealing substrate capture and release during an ordered ATPase cycle.
englishSummary: AFG3L2, located in the mitochondrial inner membrane, is an ATP-fueled protease responsible for protein degradation, and its dysfunction has been implicated in multiple neurodegenerative disorders. However, the structural basis underlying its ATP-driven substrate translocation remains incompletely understood. Here, we purified full-length human AFG3L2 and determined its cryo-EM structures in four distinct conformational states (Con1-Con4), revealing substrate engagement in the core catalytic domain despite weak EM density for its transmembrane domain.

title: Association of completion imaging modalities and carotid endarterectomy outcomes in the Vascular Quality Initiative.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Completion imaging after carotid endarterectomy (CEA) confirms technical success and identifies defects requiring correction. However, the comparative effectiveness of imaging modalities in detecting clinically significant problems remains unclear. This study evaluated completion imaging patterns, intraoperative re-exploration as a surrogate for detection efficacy, and associated postoperative outcomes.

METHODS: CEAs performed between 2012 and 2024 in the Vascular Quality Initiative were analyzed. Completion imaging was categorized as none, Doppler, duplex ultrasound, or angiography. Intraoperative re-exploration rates were compared across modalities to assess detection of technical defects requiring revision. Postoperative outcomes were analyzed among patients who required re-exploration. Inverse probability weighted logistic regression estimated adjusted odds ratios (aOR). Temporal trends were also analyzed.

RESULTS: Among 208,786 CEAs, 24% had no completion imaging, 48% used Doppler, 24% duplex, and 4% angiography. Angiography had the highest intraoperative re-exploration rate (none, 0.9%; Doppler, 0.9%; duplex, 2.3%; angiography, 3.6%; P < .001). Among the 2723 patients who required re-exploration, postoperative stroke occurred in 8.3% with no imaging, 12.5% with Doppler, 3.7% with duplex, and 22.5% with angiography (P < .001). In inverse probability weighted-adjusted analyses, intraoperative duplex was associated with significant reduction in postoperative stroke compared with: no imaging [aOR, 0.43; 95% confidence interval (CI), 0.27-0.69], Doppler (aOR, 0.28; 95% CI, 0.19-0.40), and angiography (aOR, 0.13; 95% CI, 0.09-0.20), all P < .001. Overall, angiography had the worst stroke outcomes. Doppler and angiography performed worse than duplex across additional end points, including ipsilateral stroke, transient ischemic attack, any neurological event, return to operating room, and 30-day mortality. Despite the stronger safety profile of duplex, it remains underused, as most CEAs performed in the last 15 years have used Doppler or no imaging.

CONCLUSIONS: Re-exploration and stroke outcomes after completion imaging reflect each modality's safety and efficacy in detecting significant technical defects. Duplex ultrasound demonstrated the lowest stroke rates and overall complications compared with angiography, Doppler, and no imaging, suggesting its superior efficacy and safety. Doppler showed intermediate performance, whereas angiography carried the highest risk among patients who required re-exploration. Despite strong evidence favoring duplex, the majority of surgeons performing CEAs still rely on Doppler or omit any completion imaging. Greater use of duplex ultrasound and incorporation of intraoperative duplex assessment into vascular training may improve intraoperative assessment, although further prospective evaluation is warranted.
englishSummary: OBJECTIVE: Completion imaging after carotid endarterectomy (CEA) confirms technical success and identifies defects requiring correction. However, the comparative effectiveness of imaging modalities in detecting clinically significant problems remains unclear. This study evaluated completion imaging patterns, intraoperative re-exploration as a surrogate for detection efficacy, and associated postoperative outcomes.

title: Variation and temporal trends in Medicare Severity Diagnosis Related Group billing for carotid endarterectomy across Vascular Quality Initiative centers.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hospitals use Medicare Severity Diagnosis Related Group (MS-DRG) coding to bill for each admission, with higher payment provided for those with complications or comorbidities (CCs) or major CCs (MCCs). We analyzed variation in MS-DRG coding for carotid endarterectomy (CEA) across Vascular Quality Initiative (VQI) centers to identify opportunities for improvement.

METHODS: We matched CEA cases in the VQI registry with Medicare claims data from 2013 through 2023. A multivariable stepwise logistic regression model was created to identify variables associated with CC or MCC billing (with odds ratios [ORs]). We examined variations in CC or MCC billing percentages among centers and applied a multivariable model to compare observed-to-expected (O:E) CC or MCC billing rates to adjust for patient differences. Billing trends over time were analyzed using linear regression.

RESULTS: Among 75,064 primary CEA admissions for Medicare beneficiaries, 39.5% were billed with CCs or MCCs (31.1% CCs, 8.4% MCCs) and 60.5% without. Eleven VQI clinical variables that indicated CCs were significantly associated with CC or MCC billing: dialysis dependence (OR, 22.30), postoperative neurological events (OR, 5.25), length of stay >2 days (OR, 4.98), pre-existing heart failure (OR, 4.08), any postoperative complication (OR, 3.70), reoperation (OR, 3.65), preoperative neurological event (OR, 1.70), higher American Society of Anesthesiologists class (OR, 1.50), urgent/emergent procedure (OR, 1.28), postoperative intravenous blood pressure management (OR, 1.27), and institutional transfer (OR, 1.16). Across 371 VQI centers, CC or MCC billing rates varied 5.6-fold, ranging from 15% to 84% of admissions. After risk adjustment, observed-to-expected ratios still demonstrated 4.2-fold variation, from 0.45 to 1.90 across centers. The observed rate of CC or MCC billing increased over time, from 35.5% in 2015 to 46.1% in 2023 (P < .001). In contrast, the expected adjusted rates predicted by the model remained stable (P = .269). A discrete inflection point was identified between 2016 and 2017, after which higher billing rates persisted (P < .001).

CONCLUSIONS: Substantial variation exists for MS-DRG billing for CEA across VQI centers. Billing rates for CCs or MCCs increased from 2013 through 2023. These findings suggest potential underbilling at some centers and overbilling at others. Leveraging Medicare-linked VQI registry data and the proposed model could help to improve coding and billing accuracy, optimize reimbursement, and reduce Medicare audit risk.
englishSummary: BACKGROUND: Hospitals use Medicare Severity Diagnosis Related Group (MS-DRG) coding to bill for each admission, with higher payment provided for those with complications or comorbidities (CCs) or major CCs (MCCs). We analyzed variation in MS-DRG coding for carotid endarterectomy (CEA) across Vascular Quality Initiative (VQI) centers to identify opportunities for improvement. METHODS: We matched CEA cases in the VQI registry with Medicare claims data from 2013 through 2023.

title: Arterial Blood Gas and Arterial Lines.
abstract: Arterial blood gas sampling and arterial line placement are essential bedside procedures in the care of critically ill patients. This article reviews the indications, contraindications, and preprocedural assessment for arterial access, including surface anatomy, ultrasound guidance, and site selection considerations. In particular, the article highlights differences between peripheral and central cannulation. Step-by-step procedural techniques are described for both sampling and arterial catheter insertion at radial, brachial, axillary, and femoral sites. The article also addresses equipment setup, specimen handling, postprocedure monitoring, troubleshooting, and documentation and billing considerations.

title: Modern Open Surgical Methods for Central Venous Occlusion.
abstract: Central venous occlusion (CVO) continues to pose a significant clinical challenge, especially in hemodialysis patients or those presenting with challenging anatomy. Endovascular approaches continue to improve and are first-line treatments, but open surgical approaches remain a viable option for cases that aren't amenable to endovascular therapy. Despite advances in sharp recanalization techniques, high-pressure balloon angioplasty, and covered/uncovered stents, endovascular interventions demonstrate limited primary patency, with rates declining at 12 months, necessitating frequent reinterventions. In this review, we focus on selected current surgical options for patients with central venous occlusions. There are many surgical options for dialysis patients with central venous occlusion. In this paper, we'll focus on HeRO graft placement and axillary vein to-right atrial bypass. Emphasis is placed on technical feasibility, patency outcomes, and anatomical profile. While surgical bypass procedures demonstrate comparable or superior long-term secondary patency to endovascular approaches, success requires regular surveillance and a proactive strategy for managing graft-related complications. Understanding the role of open surgical techniques is essential for providing comprehensive care in dialysis patients with advanced central venous disease.

title: May - Thurner syndrome: a case report of a lethal undiagnosed left iliac vein thrombosis.
abstract: May-Thurner syndrome (MTS), also known as iliac vein compression syndrome, is a pro-thrombotic condition caused by the compression of the left iliac vein by the right common iliac artery, often resulting in deep vein thrombosis (DVT). MTS accounts for 2-5% of all DVT cases and is often underdiagnosed due to the difficulty of assessing the deep pelvic veins. We present the case of a 63-year-old female with a history of Crohn's disease and scoliosis, who developed lower limb pain and venous ulcers. Despite negative Doppler ultrasound and exclusion of other conditions such as diabetes and vasculitis, the patient deteriorated after a fall, leading to cardiogenic shock and death. Autopsy revealed a thrombus in the left iliac vein and an embolus in the inferior vena cava, causing fatal venous obstruction. Histological examination confirmed thrombotic formations in both sites and assigned the iliac thrombus to phase III of thrombus organization, indicating that it predated the terminal event by several days. This case underscores the importance of comprehensive evaluation in patients with lower limb ulcers and pain, as Doppler ultrasound alone may not detect deeper venous abnormalities such as MTS. Advanced imaging techniques, including multi-detector computed tomography venography or magnetic resonance venography, may be necessary to diagnose MTS in such cases, preventing life-threatening complications.

MTS accounts for 2-5% of all DVT cases and is often underdiagnosed due to the difficulty of assessing the deep pelvic veins. We present the case of a 63-year-old female with a history of Crohn's disease and scoliosis, who developed lower limb pain and venous ulcers.

title: Penile Necrosis in a Patient With End-Stage Kidney Disease: Suspected Uremic Calciphylaxis in the Setting of Severe Peripheral Arterial Disease.
abstract: Uremic calciphylaxis, also known as calcific uremic arteriolopathy, is a rare and potentially fatal complication of advanced kidney disease. Penile involvement is uncommon and may result in progressive tissue necrosis. In patients with end-stage kidney disease, penile necrosis may have multiple contributing etiologies, including calciphylaxis, severe peripheral arterial disease, diabetic vasculopathy, and infection. A 68-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease receiving continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis, longstanding diabetes mellitus, severe peripheral arterial disease, profound hypoalbuminemia, and abnormalities in mineral metabolism presented with extensive necrosis involving the penis, left hemiscrotum, and lower extremities. Laboratory evaluation demonstrated severe hypoalbuminemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, anemia, and leukocytosis. A sputum culture grew extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae, while a urine culture grew ESBL-producing Escherichia coli. These microbiological findings documented respiratory and urinary isolates, respectively, but did not establish infection of the necrotic genital or lower-extremity tissues. The patient underwent right above-knee amputation and total penectomy with perineal urethrostomy. Despite surgical removal of grossly necrotic tissue, ischemic changes persisted, followed by amputation stump wound dehiscence, hemodynamic deterioration, septic shock, acute respiratory failure, and death. The coexistence of end-stage kidney disease requiring peritoneal dialysis, longstanding diabetes mellitus, severe peripheral arterial disease, profound hypoalbuminemia, mineral abnormalities, and multisite tissue necrosis raised substantial clinical suspicion for uremic calciphylaxis. However, the absence of histopathological confirmation, documented radiological evidence of vascular calcification, and intact parathyroid hormone measurement precluded a definitive diagnosis. The tissue necrosis was considered multifactorial, with severe peripheral arterial disease, diabetic vasculopathy, infection, and suspected uremic calciphylaxis representing potential contributors.

Penile involvement is uncommon and may result in progressive tissue necrosis. In patients with end-stage kidney disease, penile necrosis may have multiple contributing etiologies, including calciphylaxis, severe peripheral arterial disease, diabetic vasculopathy, and infection.

title: Patient-specific finite element modeling of image-derived shell morphoelastic growth: A general framework and application to stented aortic dissection.
abstract: Vascular pathology often manifests in complex shape evolution visualized by longitudinal computed tomography (CT) imaging. Growth and remodeling (G&R) frameworks have been integrated into finite element (FE) modeling to probe the mechanics underlying this progression, extending into patient-specific approaches. Their scalability and translatability, however, are limited by the computational burden associated with heterogeneous, anisotropic growth fields and through-thickness meshing. While existing shell growth formulations can mitigate this burden, they require nontrivial FE implementation especially in commercial softwares (e.g., Abaqus) and their efficacy in patient-specific geometries under complex loading is unclear. In this work, we present a general computational framework to implement shell morphoelastic growth computed directly from registered patient-specific CT images. This shell implementation is validated against solid 3D formulations, allows thickness tunability, and increases compatibility with CT surfaces. We demonstrate the robustness of this formulation through modeling post-operative growth in a patient-specific aortic dissection under stent-based loading. Results first show that complex stent-based loading can deform the shell dissection flap to reproduce post-operative geometry. The outer aortic wall is then given a growth field calculated from registration of 1-month and 5-year post-operative CT images, which is implemented along with stent-based loading and pressurization. Results from this model capture the trends in total and lumen morphological evolution observed at intermediate timepoints. These findings establish a general framework, validated with a patient-specific case study of aortic dissection, with the potential to expand to other complex systems, scale to larger patient populations, and apply G&R to clinical translation.

Growth and remodeling (G&R) frameworks have been integrated into finite element (FE) modeling to probe the mechanics underlying this progression, extending into patient-specific approaches. Their scalability and translatability, however, are limited by the computational burden associated with heterogeneous, anisotropic growth fields and through-thickness meshing.

title: Central Venous Access.
abstract: Central venous catheterization (CVC) is a commonly performed procedure in which an indwelling catheter is placed within a central vein to facilitate administration of vasoactive medications, chemotherapy, parenteral nutrition, and extracorporeal therapies, as well as hemodynamic monitoring. This article reviews the indications and contraindications for CVC placement, bleeding risk considerations, and factors influencing site selection. Methods for confirming catheter position, including sonographic and radiographic approaches, are discussed. Mechanical, thrombotic, and infectious complications are reviewed, along with strategies for prevention and postprocedural monitoring. Common technical and sonographic pitfalls encountered during CVC placement are also highlighted.

title: Peripheral Venous Access.
abstract: Peripheral venous access is the most common invasive procedure performed in hospitalized patients. In this review, the authors explore ultrasound-guided peripheral venous access, including peripheral intravenous catheters, midline catheters, and peripherally inserted central catheters. Indications, contraindications, and anticipated duration of therapy for each device are summarized based on current literature. Strategies to optimize cannulation success, including vessel assessment, catheter-to-vein ratio, and appropriate device selection, are reviewed. Complications such as early device failure, thrombosis, infection, and vessel injury are also discussed.

title: Feasibility and Restenosis Predictors of Optical Frequency Domain Imaging-Guided Drug-Coated Balloon Treatment for Femoropopliteal Lesions.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The clinical utility of optical frequency domain imaging (OFDI) for guiding endovascular therapy in femoropopliteal lesions has not been established. Additionally, the prognostic value of OFDI findings during drug-coated balloon (DCB) treatment for femoropopliteal lesions has never been evaluated.

OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to clarify the feasibility of OFDI-guided DCB treatment and investigate the OFDI findings associated with restenosis after DCB treatment in femoropopliteal lesions.

METHODS: This multicenter, prospective, observational study included patients with symptomatic, nonseverely calcified femoropopliteal lesions who underwent DCB treatment under OFDI guidance. Procedural success was defined as residual stenosis of less than 30% without flow compromise and without any procedural complications. The primary outcome was restenosis of the target lesion, defined as a peak systolic velocity ratio of ≥2.5, as measured by duplex ultrasound at rest or target lesion revascularization.

RESULTS: A total of 202 lesions were initially enrolled, of which 35 (17.3%) were excluded primarily because of severe calcification or inadequate OFDI data. Among the 167 analyzable lesions included in the present analysis, the procedural success rate and 1-year freedom from restenosis were 91.6% and 85.5%, respectively. In the procedural OFDI findings, a calcified nodule in the target lesion (subdistribution hazard ratio: 3.25; 95% CI: 1.01-10.42; P = 0.048) was associated with restenosis.

CONCLUSIONS: OFDI-guided DCB treatment is feasible in selected femoropopliteal lesions. An OFDI-detected calcified nodule is associated with an increased risk of restenosis after DCB treatment for femoropopliteal lesions.
englishSummary: BACKGROUND: The clinical utility of optical frequency domain imaging (OFDI) for guiding endovascular therapy in femoropopliteal lesions has not been established. Additionally, the prognostic value of OFDI findings during drug-coated balloon (DCB) treatment for femoropopliteal lesions has never been evaluated. OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to clarify the feasibility of OFDI-guided DCB treatment and investigate the OFDI findings associated with restenosis after DCB treatment in femoropopliteal lesions.

title: Predictive value of combined cerebral blood volume index and systemic inflammation indices for 90-day functional outcomes following endovascular treatment in patients with acute ischemic stroke and proximal large vessel occlusion: machine learning model construction and population attributable fraction analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: We investigated whether the cerebral blood volume (CBV) index and pretreatment systemic inflammatory indices (SIIs) provide complementary prognostic information for 90-day functional outcomes after successful endovascular therapy (EVT) for anterior circulation large vessel occlusion and evaluated the advantages of machine learning models in terms of prognostic outcomes and quantified adverse outcomes using the population attributable fraction (PAF).

METHODS: This retrospective analysis of a prospective registry included 474 patients who were treated between November 2020 and June 2024. An independent 53-patient multicenter cohort was used for external validation. SIIs were calculated from the first venous sample obtained at presentation, before intravenous thrombolysis, and before arterial puncture for EVT. Multivariate logistic regression and eight predictive algorithms were evaluated. PAF estimates were considered exploratory.

RESULTS: Among 474 patients, 41.6% and 28.5% achieved favorable and excellent outcomes, respectively. Higher CBV indices were more frequent among patients with favorable outcomes, whereas higher inflammatory indices were associated with worse outcomes. Logistic regression showed the highest AUC for mRS 0-2 (0.868, 95% CI 0.806-0.929), while SVM had the highest AUC for mRS 0-1 (0.839, 95% CI 0.764-0.915). The external validation AUCs were 0.816 and 0.802. PAF analysis indicated that improving the CBV index increased favorable and excellent outcomes by 97.2% and 74.8%, respectively, whereas reducing inflammatory overactivation improved them by 22.4%-39.7% and 51.2%-59.5%, respectively.

CONCLUSION: Baseline CBV index and pretreatment SII values provided complementary prognostic information after successful EVT. However, prospective validation in a broader population is required before clinical implementation.

METHODS: This retrospective analysis of a prospective registry included 474 patients who were treated between November 2020 and June 2024. An independent 53-patient multicenter cohort was used for external validation.

title: Perioperative Risk Factors and Development of a Clinical Risk Score for Postoperative Acute Kidney Injury in Patients Undergoing Lower Limb Amputation for Vascular Disease.
abstract: Introduction Perioperative acute kidney injury (AKI) is a recognised complication of vascular surgery and is associated with adverse short- and long-term outcomes. Various perioperative factors, including pre-existing comorbidities, baseline kidney function, intraoperative haemodynamic changes, vasopressor use, and nephrotoxic medications, may contribute to the development of postoperative AKI. However, data addressing AKI specifically in patients undergoing lower limb amputation remain limited. This study aimed to evaluate perioperative risk factors and develop a risk scoring model to predict postoperative AKI in this population. Methods Data from 101 patients were collected using HIVE (Epic Systems Corporation, Verona, Wisconsin, USA), a trust-wide electronic patient record (EPR) system used in Manchester Royal Infirmary, Manchester NHS Foundation Trust. Data were extracted across two phases, preoperative and intraoperative. Data were then imported onto Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS; IBM Corp., Armonk, New York, USA) software for further analysis. Following this, relevant variables were used to develop a risk prediction model and identify risk factors. Results Postoperative AKI was observed in 12.8% of the patients (n=13). The development of postoperative AKI with statistical significance was observed in patients with higher baseline serum creatinine level, low estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) as well as patients with comorbidities like heart failure and chronic kidney disease (CKD). Based on the identified risk factors, points were assigned proportional to their odds ratio and a simplified risk calculation model was developed that stratify patient into low, medium or high risk. Discussion This simplified risk scoring model allows for rapid classification of patients into low-, medium- or high-risk categories. Notably, risk increases substantially across categories, reinforcing the model's clinical utility: 5.88% in low-, 38.46% in medium-, and 100% in high-risk patients. This contrast underscores the significant role that risk stratification plays in clinical decision-making. Having a risk score could be invaluable in guiding early interventions prior to surgery, potentially reducing postoperative AKI risk. One limitation of the model is the potential impact of loss of muscle mass following amputation, which may affect the accuracy of postoperative serum creatinine measurements, impacting the assessment of kidney function.
englishSummary: Introduction Perioperative acute kidney injury (AKI) is a recognised complication of vascular surgery and is associated with adverse short- and long-term outcomes. Various perioperative factors, including pre-existing comorbidities, baseline kidney function, intraoperative haemodynamic changes, vasopressor use, and nephrotoxic medications, may contribute to the development of postoperative AKI. However, data addressing AKI specifically in patients undergoing lower limb amputation remain limited.

title: A Vascular Surgery and Primary Care Partnership for Improving Resident Training in Peripheral Artery Disease Management.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Early diagnosis, establishment of best medical management, and timely specialty referral for patients with peripheral artery disease (PAD) remain ongoing challenges. In this study, we sought to identify gaps in internal medicine (IM) and family medicine (FM) residents' self-rated competency of PAD management and investigated whether an educational session led by vascular surgeons could promote recognition and confidence in patient care.

METHODS: A single educational session, featuring a PowerPoint presentation, hands-on training (pulse and Doppler examination), and open discussion, was offered to IM and FM residents on two separate occasions. A presession survey assessed self-rated knowledge, practices, attitudes, and medical training regarding PAD, followed by a truncated postsession survey. The responses were grouped as high versus moderate/low. Descriptive statistics and the McNemar Exact test were used for paired sample comparison.

RESULTS: Thirty-one residents completed both surveys (65% IM, 35% FM, 58% male, and 77% first- or second-year trainees). Presession data revealed gaps in knowledge with few residents rating their understanding as "high". Postsession, there was a significant increase across all measured areas (P < 0.001). Notably, improvements were seen in the number of residents who felt highly confident in diagnosing PAD (from 16.1% to 90.3%), using a vascular Doppler (6.5% to 83.9%), ordering noninvasive testing (from 6.5% to 83.9%), performing a lower extremity pulse exam (from 12.9% to 87.1%), managing PAD for amputation prevention (from 12.9% to 71.0%), and referring to a vascular specialist (from 25.8% to 83.9%).

CONCLUSION: Resident knowledge and confidence improved significantly as a result of a singular educational session. This collaborative model between vascular surgery educators and primary care residency programs demonstrates an adaptable framework that successfully addresses a gap in PAD management training.

title: Calibrated Microspheres versus Liquid Embolic Agents for Chronic Subdural Hematoma: A Single-Center Clinicoradiologic Analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Middle meningeal artery embolization (MMAe) is an effective treatment for chronic subdural hematoma (cSDH), but the optimal embolic agent remains debated. Landmark randomized trials predominantly used liquid embolics, although calibrated microspheres remain widely used. We compared clinicoradiologic outcomes after MMAe with 75 μm Embozene microspheres versus liquid embolics (n-butyl cyanoacrylate or Onyx 18).

METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed single-agent MMAe for cSDH at a tertiary center (January 2019-January 2025). The embolized MMA was the unit of analysis; agent choice was discretionary. The efficacy cohort required 2-8 week imaging (n = 66); the safety cohort included all single-agent procedures (n = 67; 35 particle, 32 liquid). Primary outcomes were embolization failure and unplanned surgical evacuation. Secondary outcomes included early SDH thickness, midline shift, and latest modified Rankin scale (mRS).

RESULTS: Fifty patients underwent 66 embolizations (16 bilateral): 34 particle and 32 liquid. Embolization failure occurred in 5/34 versus 4/32, and unplanned evacuation in 3/34 versus 1/32; events were few and the comparison underpowered. Female patients were more frequent in the particle group (47% vs. 19%, P = 0.020). Early SDH thickness was 8 (6) versus 6 (6) mm (P = 0.340). The safety cohort had one fatal posterior-circulation infarct after Embozene (1/35 vs. 0/32) and no other periprocedural complications.

CONCLUSIONS: Embolization failure was similar between 75 μm Embozene and liquid embolics, while unplanned evacuation was numerically higher with particles. Given infrequent events, limited sample size, and baseline imbalances, agent selection may be individualized by anatomy, visualization, and operator experience.

Landmark randomized trials predominantly used liquid embolics, although calibrated microspheres remain widely used. We compared clinicoradiologic outcomes after MMAe with 75 μm Embozene microspheres versus liquid embolics (n-butyl cyanoacrylate or Onyx 18).

title: Multistage management of pediatric septic aortoiliac disease: 6-year outcomes after endovascular repair of a common iliac artery infective native pseudoaneurysm.
abstract: Pediatric infective native arterial aneurysms are rare, and septic embolization causing aortoiliac occlusion with delayed pseudoaneurysm formation is uncommon. We describe an 11-year-old boy with pneumococcal infective endocarditis at age 4, complicated by septic embolization to the aortic bifurcation requiring open thrombectomy, who later developed a right common iliac artery infective native pseudoaneurysm. Given the high risk of repeat open reconstruction, endovascular repair used bilateral kissing balloon-expandable stent grafts with self-expanding stent graft extensions. At 6-year follow-up, he had durable pseudoaneurysm exclusion without recurrent infection; late in-stent stenosis was treated with balloon angioplasty. This case illustrates complementary roles for open and endovascular repair in pediatric aortoiliac disease.

title: Cause-Specific Endovascular Thrombectomy Time Windows in Basilar Artery Occlusion: ATTENTION Trial Post Hoc Analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) outperforms best medical treatment (BMT) for basilar artery occlusion (BAO), but the influence of stroke cause on the time sensitivity of EVT remains unclear. We hypothesized nonatherosclerotic BAO would require earlier EVT, whereas atherosclerotic BAO-with chronic stenosis and more robust collaterals-would retain EVT benefit in extended windows. We conducted a post hoc 3-way interaction analysis of the ATTENTION trial (Trial of Endovascular Treatment of Acute Basilar Artery Occlusion) to explore cause-specific EVT time patterns.

METHODS: Using randomized ATTENTION trial data (36 Chinese centers, 2021-2022), patients were stratified by onset-to-puncture time (<6 versus ≥6 hours) and TOAST (Trial of ORG 10172 in Acute Stroke Treatment) cause (atherosclerotic: large-artery atherosclerosis; nonatherosclerotic: cardioembolism/undetermined/other causes). The primary outcome was 90-day favorable functional outcome (modified Rankin Scale score 0-3), with relative risk as the primary estimand; the 3-way interaction was tested via joint Wald test. A weighted 1-hour interval odds ratio trend analysis served as an exploratory tool, with multivariable regression adjusting for confounders.

RESULTS: Among 340 patients (226 EVT+BMT, 114 BMT), for onset-to-puncture time <6 hours, patients with nonatherosclerotic BAO who received EVT achieved a significantly higher favorable outcome rate (46.7% versus 20.4%; relative risk, 2.29 [95% CI, 1.25-4.18]; P=0.007); the atherosclerotic group showed numerical outcome benefit (40.4% versus 26.1%, P=0.259). For onset-to-puncture time ≥6 hours, the numerical benefit in the atherosclerotic group increased from 14.3% to 30.6% (56.9% versus 26.3%; P=0.199), accompanied by ordinal modified Rankin Scale score improvement (common odds ratio, 3.30 [95% CI, 1.13-9.62]; P=0.029) and National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score reduction; the benefit in the nonatherosclerotic group decreased from 26.3% to 17.8% with loss of significance (39.5% versus 21.7%, P=0.341). The treatment time×cause interaction was not significant (P=0.662). The weighted 1-hour interval odds ratio trend analysis identified a provisional 5.3-hour reference point in nonatherosclerotic BAO.

CONCLUSIONS: Compared with nonatherosclerotic BAO, atherosclerotic BAO appears less time-sensitive, potentially retaining EVT responsiveness over longer windows. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require prospective validation.

title: Comparison of DOAC Versus VKA for Cerebral Venous Thrombosis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cerebral venous thrombosis is an uncommon cause of stroke that primarily affects young adults. Several clinical trials and observational studies have compared vitamin K antagonists (VKAs) with direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) for treating cerebral venous thrombosis, but the small sample sizes limit the ability to draw firm conclusions.

METHODS: We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials and observational studies comparing DOACs with VKAs for the treatment of cerebral venous thrombosis. Studies published between January 2007 and July 2025 were included. Prespecified subgroup analyses were conducted by study design, DOAC class (anti-factor Xa inhibitors versus direct thrombin inhibitors), and VKA. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk-of-Bias Tool 2 for randomized trials and the Risk of Bias in Nonrandomized Studies of Interventions for observational studies. Pooled risk ratios (RRs) with 95% CIs were calculated using random-effects models.

RESULTS: Fourteen studies (8 randomized clinical trials [RCTs] and 6 observational studies) were included. Among 3698 patients, 1669 (45.1%) received DOACs and 2029 (54.9%) received VKAs. Rates of recurrent venous thromboembolism (10.24% versus 10.99%), major bleeding (4.26% versus 6.18%), clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding (2.63% versus 1.66%), good functional outcomes (95.09% versus 89.25%), and mortality (3.37% versus 3.30%) were similar in DOACs and VKAs. Recurrent venous thromboembolism was similar between DOACs and VKAs in RCTs (RR, 1.06 [95% CI, 0.35-3.24]) and in the overall pooled analysis of all studies (RR, 0.92 [95% CI, 0.55-1.53]). Major bleeding did not differ between DOACs and VKAs in RCTs (RR, 0.73 [95% CI, 0.24-2.22]) or in the overall analysis (RR, 0.74 [95% CI, 0.44-1.25]; P=0.26). Clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding was also comparable in RCTs (RR, 1.06 [95% CI, 0.25-4.48]) and overall (RR, 1.22 [95% CI, 0.38-3.86]). Good functional outcomes (modified Rankin Scale score of 0-2) were similar between DOACs and VKAs in RCTs (RR, 1.00 [95% CI, 0.84-1.19]) and in the combined analysis of all studies (RR, 1.02 [95% CI, 0.93-1.11]). Mortality was similar between DOACs and VKAs in RCTs (RR, 1.15 [95% CI, 0.28-4.68]) and in the pooled analysis. When direct thrombin inhibitors were compared with factor Xa inhibitors, there were no significant differences in outcomes.

CONCLUSIONS: DOACs demonstrated comparable efficacy and safety to VKAs in the treatment of cerebral venous thrombosis. These findings support the use of DOACs as a reasonable alternative.
englishSummary: BACKGROUND: Cerebral venous thrombosis is an uncommon cause of stroke that primarily affects young adults. Several clinical trials and observational studies have compared vitamin K antagonists (VKAs) with direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) for treating cerebral venous thrombosis, but the small sample sizes limit the ability to draw firm conclusions. METHODS: We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials and observational studies comparing DOACs with VKAs for the treatment of cerebral venous thrombosis.

title: Postoperative recruitment and remodeling of middle meningeal artery collaterals in adult moyamoya disease: implications for preservation during combined revascularization.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The middle meningeal artery (MMA) may provide pre-existing transdural flow and postoperative collateral recruitment in adult moyamoya disease (MMD). We evaluated MMA remodeling, recruitment, and the safety relevance of preserving visible branches during combined revascularization.

METHODS: This retrospective hemisphere-level study included 110 operated hemispheres from 85 adults undergoing superficial temporal artery-middle cerebral artery bypass with encephaloduromyosynangiosis. Preoperative angiography showed visible MMA collaterals in 38 hemispheres and none in 72. Outcomes included vessel diameters, MMA caliber change ratio (MMA-CCR), Matsushima grade, and perioperative infarction. Groups were further classified by intraoperative MMA preservation or injury and by postoperative recruitment.

RESULTS: Hemispheres with visible preoperative collaterals had more advanced Suzuki stages (P < 0.001), larger postoperative MMA diameters (P = 0.006), and smaller postoperative donor superficial temporal artery diameters (P < 0.001). Among collateral-absent hemispheres, 56/72 (77.8%) developed postoperative MMA collaterals. Recruited hemispheres had better Matsushima grades (P = 0.001), larger preoperative (3.05 ± 1.14 vs 2.23 ± 1.19 mm; P = 0.016) and postoperative MMA diameters (P < 0.001), and higher MMA-CCR values (P < 0.001). Perioperative infarction occurred in 3/10 hemispheres with MMA injury and 0/28 with preservation (P = 0.014); this three-event association was exploratory.

CONCLUSION: The MMA showed postoperative recruitment and caliber remodeling. Visible branches should be preserved when technically feasible, although the observed association between injury and infarction requires validation.

We evaluated MMA remodeling, recruitment, and the safety relevance of preserving visible branches during combined revascularization. METHODS: This retrospective hemisphere-level study included 110 operated hemispheres from 85 adults undergoing superficial temporal artery-middle cerebral artery bypass with encephaloduromyosynangiosis.

title: Role of direct intraoperative ultrasound-guided renal resistive index and its association with postoperative acute kidney injury in patients undergoing abdominal vascular surgeries: A prospective cohort study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a major complication following abdominal vascular surgery, and current diagnostic markers often detect injury only after significant renal damage has occurred. Doppler-derived renal resistive index (RRI) is a promising real-time marker of renal perfusion. This study evaluated direct intraoperative ultrasound (DIOUS)-guided RRI measurement for assessing postoperative AKI in open abdominal vascular surgery.

METHODS: In this prospective study, 40 adults undergoing open abdominal vascular procedures were enroled. RRI was measured at four timepoints: preoperatively; intraoperatively, 30 minutes after aortic declamping, using DIOUS; and postoperatively at 12 and 24 hours using transabdominal Doppler ultrasonography. AKI was defined using Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes creatinine-based criteria.

RESULTS: Postoperative AKI developed in 50% of patients. Mean DIOUS-guided RRI measured 30 minutes after declamping was higher in patients who developed AKI than in those who did not (0.74 ± 0.05 vs. 0.69 ± 0.04; P = 0.003). Receiver operating characteristic analysis identified an exploratory, internally derived intraoperative RRI cut-off of 0.71, predicting postoperative AKI with 80% sensitivity and 70% specificity [area under curve 0.783; 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.639-0.927]. The odds of developing AKI increased by 33% for every 0.01-unit increase in intraoperative RRI (odds ratio 1.33; 95% CI 1.03-1.71; P = 0.026).

CONCLUSION: DIOUS-guided RRI measurement is a feasible method for real-time assessment of renal haemodynamics during open abdominal vascular surgery. The association between intraoperative RRI and postoperative AKI suggests this technique may complement perioperative renal risk assessment and support early kidney-protective interventions, pending validation in larger studies.

Doppler-derived renal resistive index (RRI) is a promising real-time marker of renal perfusion. This study evaluated direct intraoperative ultrasound (DIOUS)-guided RRI measurement for assessing postoperative AKI in open abdominal vascular surgery.

title: Endovascular repair of a true profunda femoris aneurysm.
abstract: True aneurysms of the profunda femoris artery are exceedingly rare, comprising less than 1% of all peripheral artery aneurysms. Their diagnosis is often challenging because of their atypical anatomical location and nonspecific symptoms, and rupture carries substantial morbidity. We report a patient with a history of popliteal artery aneurysm thrombosis who was subsequently found to have a 3.9 cm true aneurysm of the right profunda femoris artery. The lesion was successfully treated endovascularly with overlapping nitinol stent grafts, achieving good technical and clinical results. This represents one of the few reported cases of a true profunda femoris artery aneurysm managed by endovascular exclusion.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of magnetic resonance calcification imaging for lower-extremity peripheral artery disease.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Recent advances in magnetic resonance imaging-based bone imaging techniques may help visualize vascular calcification, and their combination with noncontrast magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) can facilitate a comprehensive, noninvasive assessment of lower-extremity peripheral artery disease (PAD) without contrast media or ionizing radiation.

METHODS: Forty-three patients with lower-extremity PAD who underwent magnetic resonance calcification imaging (MRCI) and noncontrast MRA before endovascular intervention between November 2022 and June 2024 were retrospectively analyzed. The aortoiliac and femoropopliteal arteries were divided into 10 segments on MRCI and assessed for calcification using computed tomography images as reference standards. Calcification in each segment was graded using the Peripheral Arterial Calcium Scoring System. Calcification characteristics and lumen diameters on MRCI were compared with those obtained using intravascular ultrasound (IVUS).

RESULTS: Renal insufficiency was observed in 30 of 43 patients (69.8%); 24 (55.8%) had claudication, and 16 (37.2%) had chronic limb-threatening ischemia. Weighted Cohen κ coefficients demonstrated substantial to almost perfect agreement between MRCI and computed tomography in the assessment of vascular calcification (reader 1: κ = .89; reader 2: κ = .80). In 13 patients with 24 femoropopliteal lesions (≥50% stenosis) evaluated by IVUS, MRCI demonstrated close agreement with IVUS for both calcification angles (mean difference, 1.3°; 95% limits of agreement, -19.1° to 21.8°) and lumen diameter (short axis, -0.05 mm; 95% limits of agreement, -0.46 to 0.36 mm; long axis, -0.06 mm; 95% limits of agreement, -0.67 to 0.55 mm).

CONCLUSIONS: MRCI provides quantitative, noninvasive depiction of vascular calcification, and, when combined with noncontrast MRA, may provide complementary information for the imaging assessment of lower-extremity PAD without contrast media or ionizing radiation. Future larger prospective multicenter studies are needed to confirm these findings and to further define the clinical role of this imaging approach.

METHODS: Forty-three patients with lower-extremity PAD who underwent magnetic resonance calcification imaging (MRCI) and noncontrast MRA before endovascular intervention between November 2022 and June 2024 were retrospectively analyzed. The aortoiliac and femoropopliteal arteries were divided into 10 segments on MRCI and assessed for calcification using computed tomography images as reference standards.

title: Improving Operative Note Documentation Through a Two-Cycle Clinical Audit at Sinnar Teaching Hospital, Sudan.
abstract: Introduction Operative notes are essential medical and medico-legal documents that support patient safety, postoperative management, and communication among healthcare professionals. However, compliance with recommended documentation standards frequently remains suboptimal. This study aimed to assess operative note documentation at Sinnar Teaching Hospital, Sinnar, Sudan, according to Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) guidelines and evaluate the impact of an educational intervention using a two-cycle closed-loop clinical audit. Methods A prospective, two-cycle clinical audit using total-coverage sampling was conducted in the Department of Surgery at Sinnar Teaching Hospital. A total of 500 operative notes were reviewed, including 250 notes in each audit cycle. The baseline audit was conducted between November and December 2022, followed by an educational intervention, while the re-audit was performed between July and August 2023. Data were collected using a structured checklist based on RCS guidelines. Evaluated parameters included administrative details, operative findings, technical surgical documentation, and perioperative safety measures. Descriptive statistics were used, and results were expressed as percentages. Results Overall compliance with RCS standards improved substantially from 43.8% in the baseline audit to 82.3% in the re-audit cycle. Major improvements were observed in administrative documentation, including recording of time (2% to 88%), date (14% to 97%), and elective versus emergency classification (0% to 96%). Documentation of surgical team members reached 100% compliance in the re-audit cycle. Technical operative documentation also improved, including operative procedure (40% to 84%), operative diagnosis (50% to 86%), and operative findings (74% to 90%). Safety-related documentation demonstrated improvement, with anticipated blood loss increasing from 8% to 72%, antibiotic prophylaxis from 0% to 50%, and deep vein thrombosis prophylaxis from 0% to 36%. Postoperative care instructions remained consistently high throughout both cycles (94% to 96%). Conclusion Operative note documentation at Sinnar Teaching Hospital was initially below recommended standards but improved markedly following an educational intervention. This study demonstrates that documentation quality is a modifiable aspect of surgical practice and can be significantly enhanced through structured audit-feedback and educational strategies, even in resource-limited settings. Ongoing re-audits, continuous professional education, and implementation of standardized documentation systems are recommended to sustain improvements and optimize patient safety and quality of surgical care.

title: Deep Learning-Based 3D CT Body Composition Is Associated With Mortality in Patients Undergoing Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Recent advances in artificial intelligence enable fully automated 3-dimensional computed tomography (CT)-based body composition quantification. We investigated whether automated CT-derived thoraco-abdominopelvic body composition measures are associated with mortality after transcatheter aortic valve replacement.

METHODS: In this retrospective multicenter study, consecutive patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement with preprocedural CT imaging were included between 2014 and 2023. A deep learning-based pipeline performed automated 3-dimensional segmentation of thoraco-abdominopelvic noncontrast CT scans to quantify volumes (L/m2) and attenuations (Hounsfield units) of subcutaneous adipose tissue, visceral adipose tissue, muscular adipose tissue, and lean skeletal muscle, indexed to body surface area. Associations with mortality were evaluated using Cox models and Harrell C statistics, adjusting for demographics (age, sex, body mass index) and cardiometabolic risk factors (hypertension, diabetes, chronic renal failure).

RESULTS: Among 915 patients (median age, 84 years [interquartile range, 77-90]; 58% men), 160 (17.5%) died over a median follow-up of 22 months (interquartile range, 14-36). Restricted cubic spline analyses demonstrated that lower subcutaneous adipose tissue volume and higher adipose tissue attenuation were associated with increased mortality, whereas higher skeletal muscle volume and attenuation were associated with improved survival. Addition of body composition measures provided incremental discriminatory value beyond demographics and cardiometabolic risk factors (Harrell C, 0.66 versus 0.71; P<0.001).

CONCLUSIONS: Automated 3-dimensional CT-derived body composition measures provide independent prognostic information and improve risk stratification for mortality after transcatheter aortic valve replacement. Low subcutaneous adipose tissue volume and higher adipose tissue attenuation identify patients at increased risk, whereas higher skeletal muscle volume and attenuation are associated with lower mortality.

title: A Case Report of Lichen Amyloidosis.
abstract: Lichen amyloidosis (LA) is a primary localized cutaneous amyloidosis that closely resembles other chronic dermatological disorders, potentially delaying diagnosis. We report the case of a 60-year-old man with hypertension and chronic kidney disease who was admitted in 2020 with left leg pain and swelling. Investigations ruled out deep vein thrombosis, while CT revealed diffuse subcutaneous edema. Cellulitis was suspected, and the patient was subsequently discharged with analgesia and outpatient follow-up with vascular surgery and dermatology. From 2021 onward, his symptoms were attributed to stasis eczema and lymphedema. Clinical examination revealed multiple hyperpigmented papules on the left lower limb, with additional involvement of the upper back, trunk, and arms. Laboratory investigations showed an eosinophil count of 20.2%, baseline creatinine levels, and normal electrolyte and liver function tests. Due to persistent symptoms, a skin biopsy was obtained from a lesion on the lower back. Histopathological examination revealed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, elongated rete ridges, increased melanin deposition, and superficial perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrates with melanophages. Amyloid globules within the widened papillary dermis stained positively with Congo red, confirming the diagnosis of LA. This case highlights how LA may be misdiagnosed as stasis eczema or lymphedema for years. LA should be considered in patients presenting with persistent hyperpigmentation and papular eruptions involving the lower limbs.

We report the case of a 60-year-old man with hypertension and chronic kidney disease who was admitted in 2020 with left leg pain and swelling. Investigations ruled out deep vein thrombosis, while CT revealed diffuse subcutaneous edema.

title: An evaluation of a newly implemented stroke team activation protocol in Manitoba.
abstract:
PURPOSE: The purpose of this study was to evaluate a revised stroke 25 protocol in Manitoba, which integrated Stroke Team Activation by the Virtual Emergency Care and Transfer Resource Service (VECTRS), and to determine whether its implementation reduced time to acute stroke treatment compared to the previous protocol.

METHODS: This retrospective chart review utilized Emergency Medical Services (EMS) data from the Winnipeg Fire Paramedic Service (WFPS) and hospital electronic medical records from the Winnipeg Health Sciences Centre (HSC), comparing 12 months before and 12 months after implementation of the revised Stroke 25 protocol. For each patient, the interval from EMS arrival at HSC to initiation of acute stroke treatment was calculated. Mean times to thrombolysis and EVT were compared between pre- and post-implementation cohorts.

RESULTS: In the pre-intervention cohort, 757 patients with suspected stroke were triaged to HSC, of whom 131 received Alteplase or Tenecteplase (TNK) and 33 underwent EVT. In the post- intervention group, 717 patients were triaged, with 110 receiving Alteplase/TNK and 30 undergoing endovascular thrombectomy (EVT). Mean time to thrombolysis decreased from 59.1 min pre- intervention to 52.8 min post- intervention, while mean time to EVT decreased from 92.2 min to 84.1 min, respectively.

CONCLUSION: Implementation of the revised Stroke 25 protocol was associated with modest reductions in absolute time to treatment for patients with acute ischemic stroke; however, while these differences were not statistically significant, the impact for these patients may still be clinically significant.

For each patient, the interval from EMS arrival at HSC to initiation of acute stroke treatment was calculated.

title: Anti-Ro-Positive Lupus-Like Multisystem Inflammatory Syndrome After BNT162b2 COVID-19 Vaccination: A Case Report.
abstract: Rare immune-mediated syndromes following COVID-19 vaccination have been described across a heterogeneous clinical spectrum. Anti-Ro/SSA-positive multisystem presentations with features of undifferentiated connective tissue disease (UCTD) or subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE) remain under-reported. A 66-year-old Caucasian man with no prior autoimmune history developed a progressive multisystem inflammatory illness approximately 14 days after receiving his second dose of the BNT162b2 (Pfizer-BioNTech) COVID-19 vaccine. Clinical features included an erythematous malar and dorsal rash, pharyngitis, geographic tongue, constitutional upset with profound fatigue, night sweats, and unintentional weight loss of 12 kg. Investigations revealed normocytic anaemia, elevated inflammatory markers, and bilateral pleural effusions. Positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET-CT) demonstrated metabolically active mediastinal, supraclavicular, and pelvic lymphadenopathy with increased bone marrow and splenic uptake. Autoimmune serology showed a positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) test and strongly positive anti-Ro/SSA antibodies, with negative anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA) antibodies, normal complement levels, and negative antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA). Extensive investigation excluded malignancy, infection, sarcoidosis, and classical systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). A lower limb deep vein thrombosis developed during hospitalisation. Systemic corticosteroids produced clear and sustained clinical and radiological improvement. The serological and clinical phenotype (anti-Ro-positive, anti-dsDNA-negative, complement-normal, without nephritis) is most consistent with UCTD or SCLE with systemic involvement rather than classical SLE. This case contributes to the emerging literature on post-vaccination autoimmunity, emphasises the importance of precise serological phenotyping, and highlights the need for structured long-term follow-up to determine whether such presentations represent transient immune dysregulation or the onset of persistent connective tissue disease.

Anti-Ro/SSA-positive multisystem presentations with features of undifferentiated connective tissue disease (UCTD) or subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (SCLE) remain under-reported. A 66-year-old Caucasian man with no prior autoimmune history developed a progressive multisystem inflammatory illness approximately 14 days after receiving his second dose of the BNT162b2 (Pfizer-BioNTech) COVID-19 vaccine.

title: Patient-Reported Outcomes and Disease-Specific Quality of Life After Surgical and Conservative Treatments for Lower Limb Varicose Veins: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Lower limb varicose veins are a common manifestation of chronic venous disease and can adversely affect physical functioning, symptom burden, and disease-specific quality of life (QoL). Although high ligation and stripping have traditionally been considered standard surgical approaches, conservative and minimally invasive options, such as compression therapy, sclerotherapy, and endovenous thermal or non-thermal techniques, have increasingly gained prominence. However, comparative evidence regarding patient-reported outcomes (PROMs) remains heterogeneous and dispersed across randomized trials. This systematic review aimed to evaluate randomized controlled trials (RCTs) published between 2016 and 2026 that compared surgical with conservative or minimally invasive interventions for lower limb varicose veins, with particular emphasis on patient-reported and disease-specific QoL outcomes. The review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement. PubMed/Medical Literature Analysis and Retrieval System Online (MEDLINE), Scopus, Web of Science, Excerpta Medica database (Embase), the Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar were searched for eligible RCTs published from January 2016 to July 2026. Studies evaluating surgical versus conservative or minimally invasive management and reporting PROMs or disease-specific QoL outcomes were included. Methodological quality was evaluated using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool. Due to substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesized narratively in accordance with Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) guidance. Fourteen RCTs met the eligibility criteria. Interventions included open surgery, endovenous laser ablation (EVLA), radiofrequency ablation (RFA), mechanochemical ablation (MOCA), cyanoacrylate adhesive closure, ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy (UGFS), and compression therapy. Improvements in disease-specific QoL and PROMs were reported from baseline in most treatment groups. However, these within-group improvements did not necessarily indicate superiority over alternative treatments. Between-group differences in QoL outcomes were generally small and inconsistent, although some trials reported differences in procedural pain, anatomical outcomes, or the need for re-intervention. Due to substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity, the findings were synthesized narratively. Surgical, conservative, and minimally invasive approaches were associated with meaningful improvements in patient-reported and disease-specific QoL, with no consistent evidence demonstrating clear superiority of one modality. Treatment decisions should therefore incorporate anatomical suitability, patient preference, procedural morbidity, potential need for re-intervention, and healthcare resource considerations alongside QoL outcomes.

Although high ligation and stripping have traditionally been considered standard surgical approaches, conservative and minimally invasive options, such as compression therapy, sclerotherapy, and endovenous thermal or non-thermal techniques, have increasingly gained prominence. However, comparative evidence regarding patient-reported outcomes (PROMs) remains heterogeneous and dispersed across randomized trials.

title: Primary Aortoduodenal Fistula: A Case Report and Recent Literature Review (2021-2025).
abstract: Primary aortoduodenal fistula (PADF) is a rare but life-threatening cause of gastrointestinal bleeding, most commonly resulting from an abdominal aortic aneurysm eroding into the duodenum. Diagnosis is particularly challenging because of its nonspecific clinical presentation and the limited sensitivity and technical challenges of endoscopy. We present the case of an 89-year-old man with significant cardiovascular comorbidities, who developed acute abdominal pain and transient malaise, followed by massive upper gastrointestinal bleeding leading to hemorrhagic shock. Initial management included aggressive resuscitation with crystalloids, vasopressors, and initiation of a massive hemorrhage protocol. Due to severe hemodynamic instability, we could not perform a computed tomography angiography (CTA), and the patient underwent emergent laparotomy. Intraoperative upper endoscopy via surgical gastrostomy revealed a fistula between the infrarenal aorta and the fourth portion of the duodenum. Surgical intervention included end-to-end aorto-aortic bypass with a prosthetic graft, and primary duodenal repair with omental interposition. The postoperative course was complicated by ischemic colitis, respiratory failure, and progressive multi-organ failure. Despite maximal supportive measures, the patient's condition deteriorated, and care was ultimately transitioned to comfort-focused management. In our review, one key finding is the increasing trend toward endovascular and hybrid approaches for managing PADF. These strategies may facilitate more rapid hemodynamic stabilization in critically ill patients. More recently, exclusively endovascular or endoscopic procedures have been reported as potential destination therapies in carefully selected cases, particularly when conventional open repair is not feasible. PADF remains a surgical emergency with a high risk of mortality. This case highlights the importance of early recognition, aggressive resuscitation, and prompt surgical intervention. Multidisciplinary collaboration and individualized decision-making, including consideration of hybrid endovascular and open techniques, are essential to optimize outcomes in this rare but catastrophic condition.

Diagnosis is particularly challenging because of its nonspecific clinical presentation and the limited sensitivity and technical challenges of endoscopy. We present the case of an 89-year-old man with significant cardiovascular comorbidities, who developed acute abdominal pain and transient malaise, followed by massive upper gastrointestinal bleeding leading to hemorrhagic shock.

title: Early and follow-up results of reinterventions for type 2 endoleak following endovascular repair of abdominal aortic aneurysm in the multicenter Reinterventions for Type 2 Endoleak study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Type II endoleak (T2EL) is frequent after endovascular abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) repair and may require reintervention in selected patients. However, the optimal treatment strategy for durable resolution remains uncertain. This study aimed to retrospectively evaluate the perioperative and long-term outcomes of T2Els' reinterventions, both endovascular and open surgical, in a large patient cohort from 20 high-volume academic centers.

METHODS: A retrospective analysis of consecutive patients undergoing first reintervention for T2ELs was conducted across 20 centers over a 10-year period. Patients requiring concomitant treatment for other endoleak types were excluded. A total of 403 patients were included. Primary outcomes included technical success, 30-day AAA-related mortality and reintervention-free survival during follow-up. Secondary outcomes were perioperative complications, early reintervention, overall survival, freedom from aneurysm-related death and rupture, freedom from recurrent endoleaks, freedom from open conversion or semiconversion in patients previously treated endovascularly and sac behavior during follow-up. Kaplan-Meier curves and Cox regression analyses were performed to analyze follow-up results.

RESULTS: Patients were predominantly male (90%) with a mean age of 77 years. Reintervention was indicated for sac enlargement in 94.5% of cases; 4% presented with rupture. Median time from endovascular AAA repair to reintervention was 4.3 years. Lumbar arteries (55%) and the inferior mesenteric artery (35%) were the main sources. Endovascular treatment was performed in 86% and open conversion/semiconversion in 14%. Technical success was 96%, with 1% mortality and 4% major complications. Overall survival was 80.5% and rupture-free survival 79.2% at 5 years. Recurrent T2EL occurred in 64.2%, and reintervention-free survival was 48.3%. Endovascular group showed significantly lower freedom from reintervention rates when compared to open conversion/semiconversion group [42.4% vs 86.8%; standard error, 0.04 vs standard error, 0.05; P < .001; log-rank, 15.9]. Conversion/semiconversion after endovascular treatment occurred in 14%. No differences were recorded comparing different fabric materials of the endograft in terms of freedom for reintervention and freedom from open surgery. A sac diameter ≥7 cm at the time of reintervention predicted further reinterventions, whereas primary open treatment improved durability.

CONCLUSIONS: Reinterventions for T2ELs are safe, with satisfactory immediate technical success and low perioperative mortality. During follow-up, risks of rupture and AAA-related death remain low. However, the endoleak recurrence rate exceeds 60% at 5 years, necessitating reintervention in over 40% of patients. Early intervention for patients with a sac diameter approaching 7 cm can be suggested, whereas a primary open approach may be considered in low-risk patients.
englishSummary: BACKGROUND: Type II endoleak (T2EL) is frequent after endovascular abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) repair and may require reintervention in selected patients. However, the optimal treatment strategy for durable resolution remains uncertain. This study aimed to retrospectively evaluate the perioperative and long-term outcomes of T2Els' reinterventions, both endovascular and open surgical, in a large patient cohort from 20 high-volume academic centers.

title: Characterizing the Thrombotic Spectrum and Clinical Phenotypes of Tranexamic Acid-Associated Adverse Events: A Pharmacovigilance Study Based on the FAERS Database.
abstract: Tranexamic acid (TXA) is widely used to reduce bleeding in surgical, trauma, obstetric, and gynecological settings. However, concerns remain regarding TXA-associated thrombotic adverse events, and their phenotypic heterogeneity and clinical severity have not been comprehensively characterized. This study investigated TXA-associated thrombotic events using the Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) from 2004Q1 to 2026Q1. Thrombotic adverse events were identified using the Standardized MedDRA Query (SMQ) "Embolic and thrombotic events" and evaluated by disproportionality analysis based on reporting odds ratios (RORs). Qualifying thrombotic events were assigned to the SMQ vessel-type subgroups-arterial, vessel-type unspecified/mixed, and venous-and demographic characteristics, indications, clinical outcomes and time-to-onset were compared across subgroups; signal strength was further related to clinical severity. In all, 515 thrombotic cases associated with TXA and 26 selected thrombotic terms were found (arterial, 157; mixed, 168; venous, 190). Venous thromboembolism-pulmonary embolism (n = 128, ROR 13.94) and deep vein thrombosis (n = 58, ROR 9.09)-is the most frequent type and brings about the most severe and fatal consequences (death reported in 16.8% of venous versus 2.5% of arterial reports), whereas the strongest disproportionality signals were observed for rare site-specific events such as ovarian vein thrombosis (ROR 352.95) and cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (ROR 118.35). The three subgroups differed markedly in demographic and clinical characteristics: venous events occurred predominantly in women (73.7%) treated for menorrhagia (35.3%), whereas arterial events arose mainly in surgical or procedural settings (intravenous route 36.3%; surgery/prophylaxis 19.1%) and presented earliest after exposure [median time-to-onset (TTO) 0 versus 7 days]. Signal strength was not concordant with clinical severity across the thrombotic spectrum. These findings provide a deeper understanding of the thrombotic safety of TXA, indicate that the clinical background may influence the phenotypic differences among the different thrombotic types, and emphasize the necessity of enhanced attention and risk stratification in high-risk groups.

title: Initial Direct Oral Anticoagulants Versus Warfarin After Cerebral Venous Thrombosis: A Target Trial Emulation.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Vitamin K antagonists have traditionally been used after cerebral venous thrombosis, whereas direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are increasingly prescribed. Whether DOACs are noninferior to warfarin for preventing 1-year symptomatic recurrent venous thromboembolism (VTE) remains uncertain.

METHODS: We conducted a registry-based target trial emulation in a bidirectional multicenter Chinese cerebral venous thrombosis registry (retrospective phase, 2015-2022; prospective phase, 2023-2025). Eligible patients were adults with imaging-confirmed cerebral venous thrombosis who initiated either a DOAC or warfarin within 30 days after diagnosis. Time zero was the date of the first oral anticoagulant prescription. The primary efficacy outcome was symptomatic recurrent VTE within 1 year. Propensity score overlap weighting was used, and weighted Fine-Gray models treated death as a competing event. The clinically acceptable noninferiority margin was defined as an absolute increase of 1.5 percentage points in 1-year recurrent VTE risk, corresponding approximately to a relative margin of 1.50 for the primary Fine-Gray analysis.

RESULTS: Among 2476 eligible patients, 942 initiated a DOAC (rivaroxaban, n=701; dabigatran, n=121; apixaban, n=113; edoxaban, n=7) and 1534 initiated warfarin. Within 1 year, symptomatic recurrent VTE occurred in 36 and 73 patients, respectively. The overlap-weighted 1-year recurrence risks were 3.74% and 5.47%, corresponding to a risk difference of -1.73 percentage points (95% CI, -3.76 to 0.30). DOAC treatment was associated with a lower subdistribution hazard ratio of 0.67 compared with that of warfarin ([95% CI, 0.37-1.21]; P=0.184), meeting the prespecified noninferiority criterion (P for noninferiority=0.004). Major bleeding was rare within 1 year (0 versus 1 patient). Clinical nonmajor bleeding occurred in 18 versus 34 patients, and any bleeding occurred in 48 versus 75 patients.

CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with cerebral venous thrombosis selected for oral anticoagulation, initial treatment with a DOAC met the noninferiority criterion relative to warfarin for the prevention of symptomatic recurrent VTE at 1 year. Findings regarding bleeding outcomes were exploratory and do not permit conclusions regarding comparative safety or equivalence.

Whether DOACs are noninferior to warfarin for preventing 1-year symptomatic recurrent venous thromboembolism (VTE) remains uncertain. METHODS: We conducted a registry-based target trial emulation in a bidirectional multicenter Chinese cerebral venous thrombosis registry (retrospective phase, 2015-2022; prospective phase, 2023-2025).

title: Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt as a Cause of Recurrent Encephalopathy in a Non-cirrhotic Patient: Successful Combined Transhepatic and Transjugular Embolization.
abstract: Intrahepatic portosystemic shunts (IPSS) are rare vascular anomalies that can cause recurrent encephalopathy in non-cirrhotic patients. We present a case of a female with recurrent episodes of delirium, in whom initial laboratory tests showed hyperammonemia with preserved hepatic function. Cross-sectional imaging revealed a left-sided IPSS connecting distal branches of the left portal vein to the left hepatic vein. Given her persistent neurocognitive symptoms despite optimal medical therapy, endovascular closure was performed using a dual-access strategy: transhepatic coil embolization of the portal afferent branches, followed by transjugular deployment of an Amplatzer plug in the venous outflow. After the procedure, the patient experienced full resolution of symptoms, with no recurrent neurological episodes during follow-up. This case highlights the importance of considering IPSS as a reversible cause of unexplained encephalopathy and supports the efficacy of combined-access embolization.

We present a case of a female with recurrent episodes of delirium, in whom initial laboratory tests showed hyperammonemia with preserved hepatic function. Cross-sectional imaging revealed a left-sided IPSS connecting distal branches of the left portal vein to the left hepatic vein.

title: Caprini Score-Guided Venous Thromboembolism Prophylaxis in Spine Instrumentation Surgery: A Comparative Analysis of Mechanical vs. Pharmacomechanical Strategies Across Etiological Subgroups.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Venous thromboembolism (VTE), encompassing deep venous thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE), is a major source of morbidity and mortality in patients undergoing spine surgery. Although various risk factors for developing VTE have been identified, pharmacological prophylaxis is used selectively in spine surgery due to the risk of epidural hematoma. We report our institutional experience with VTE prophylaxis following spine instrumentation surgery across all surgical etiologies.

METHODS: A single-center retrospective cohort study of patients ≥18 years of age who underwent spine instrumentation surgery for degenerative, traumatic, or oncologic pathologies, and patients of all ages who underwent surgery for spinal deformity over a three-year period was performed. Caprini VTE risk score was used for individual risk stratification.

RESULTS: A total of 265 patients were included: degenerative (n=174, 65.7%), trauma (n=45, 17.0%), deformity (n=33, 12.5%), and tumor (n=13, 4.9%). The overall mean age was 46.1±17.5 years, and there were 133 male patients (50.2%). Significant differences existed across groups in age (Kruskal-Wallis H=97.4, p<0.001), index procedure characteristics, and VTE risk profiles. Mechanical prophylaxis alone was employed in 212 patients (80.0%), while 53 patients (20.0%) received combined pharmacomechanical prophylaxis. No patient (0%) in the mechanical-only group developed a perioperative VTE event or postoperative hematoma. One patient (1.9%) in the combined pharmacomechanical group developed a postoperative PE, arising in the context of a preoperative proximal DVT. Firth's penalized logistic regression identified polytrauma (OR 29.0, 95% CI 3.3-3835.0; p=0.001), Caprini score ≥7 (OR 8.8, 95% CI 3.8-20.9; p<0.001), and prior VTE history (OR 61.8, 95% CI 5.7-8406.4; p<0.001) as independent predictors of combined prophylaxis receipt.

CONCLUSION: Mechanical prophylaxis, implemented as part of a structured protocol that included sequential pneumatic compression devices and standardized postoperative care, was associated with low VTE risk following spine instrumentation surgery. Individualized risk stratification using validated tools such as the Caprini score, combined with selective pharmacomechanical prophylaxis in high-risk patients, may optimize outcomes in this population. Prospective multicenter studies are needed to validate these findings.
englishSummary: BACKGROUND: Venous thromboembolism (VTE), encompassing deep venous thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE), is a major source of morbidity and mortality in patients undergoing spine surgery. Although various risk factors for developing VTE have been identified, pharmacological prophylaxis is used selectively in spine surgery due to the risk of epidural hematoma. We report our institutional experience with VTE prophylaxis following spine instrumentation surgery across all surgical etiologies.
